name: Eustache Lambert
born: c. 1617-1618, "probably near Boulogne in France" (DCB); tree: 21 Sep 1617, "Boulogne, Oise, Picardie"
died: 6 Jul 1673, Quebec, buried 7 Jul (DCB; Roy vol. 1 p. 258); tree says 6 Jun 1673
spouse: Marie Laurence, m. 1656 at Quebec (DCB gives 1656; the tree's "Boulogne" as the marriage place is wrong, he was in Canada)
place: Boulogne (Picardy) → Quebec → Sainte-Marie among the Hurons → Pointe-Lévy (Lauzon), farm "Sainte-Marie"
place_note: Pin is approximate: the Sainte-Marie farm lay between the Chaudière and the Etchemin, today's Saint-Romuald (Roy vol. 2 p. 41).
birthplace_question: Which Boulogne is unsettled. The tree says "Boulogne, Oise, Picardie". The Oise has Boulogne-la-Grasse, a village 11 km SE of Montdidier and 23 km N of Compiègne (Wikipédia), which was Picardy; Boulogne-sur-Mer is in the Boulonnais (today Pas-de-Calais), also counted as Picardy then. A Quebec genealogical chronicle says "originaire de Boulogne en Picardie" (gensdupays.ca/cercle/chroniques/20141105.pdf), which fits either. The DCB says only "near Boulogne". No baptism has been seen; Fichier Origine was not reached.
life: A layman who could not write his name (he signed with a mark), he gave himself to the Jesuits as a donné, worked and interpreted at Sainte-Marie among the Hurons, then took eight arpents of St. Lawrence shore at Pointe-Lévy in 1653, kept an eel fishery there from 1651, named the farm Sainte-Marie, and became a Quebec merchant and militia commander.

beats.title: A frontier boyhood
beats.text: Eustache was about eighteen in 1636, "the year of Corbie", when a Spanish army crossed the Somme on 5 August, took Corbie on the 15th, raided as far as Compiègne, and sent the court fleeing Paris. If his Boulogne was the village in the Oise, the invasion passed within a day's walk of it; if it was Boulogne-sur-Mer, he grew up in a walled port some twenty kilometres from the Spanish border in Artois. Either way he may have known soldiers' billets, requisitions and hungry winters before he knew anything of Canada.
sources: "First siege of Corbie", Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_siege_of_Corbie
"Boulogne-la-Grasse", Wikipédia (fr), https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boulogne-la-Grasse

"Histoire de Boulogne-sur-Mer", Wikipédia (fr), https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Histoire_de_Boulogne-sur-Mer ("la frontière se trouve à une vingtaine de kilomètres de l'entrée de Boulogne", said of 1662)

beats.title: The little books from Paris
beats.text: Every year from 1632 the Jesuits printed a Relation of their Canadian missions, almost all at Cramoisy in Paris, and they were "disseminated among the general public"; the 1639 one sent Jeanne Mance to Canada, and the Ursulines and hospital nuns who landed at Quebec that year came in answer to them. Eustache could not read, so if the Relations reached him it was aloud, from a pulpit or a priest. He may have heard of the Huron mission the way most people did: as a story read to a room.
sources: L. Pouliot, "LE JEUNE, PAUL", DCB vol. 1, https://www.biographi.ca/en/bio/le_jeune_paul_1E.html
"GUYART, MARIE (Marie de l'Incarnation)", DCB vol. 1, https://www.biographi.ca/en/bio/guyart_marie_1E.html

beats.title: Giving himself away
beats.text: The Jesuits needed men who could farm, build, hunt, nurse and, unlike their lay brothers, carry a gun. Jérôme Lalemant began taking such men as donnés in the Huron country from 1639: laymen who gave their whole lives to the mission without religious vows, for their keep and the Society's promise to look after them to the end. In 1642 Lalemant wrote that it was unjust for "young men in the flower of their youth" to give themselves to so dangerous a country on "such weak assurances of a livelihood". Eustache, in his mid-twenties, was one of them; a family biographer, writing as a novelist, says he was recruited in France and reached Quebec in 1644.
sources: "LALEMANT, JÉRÔME", DCB vol. 1, https://www.biographi.ca/en/bio/lalemant_jerome_1E.html

beats.title: Ten weeks of sea, then a rock with a fort on it
beats.text: The crossing took two months or more: Marie de l'Incarnation's ship left on 4 May 1639 and reached Quebec on 1 August, and a bad-wind passage could run sixty or seventy days. Quebec, when he came up the river, was a fort on the cliff, Champlain's old Habitation by the water below with a path between them, a Jesuit college, the new Ursuline convent and Hôtel-Dieu, and a few hundred people: 250 in 1641, about 2,000 by 1653. That spring of 1644 the Iroquois burned and killed at Cap-Rouge, just upriver. He may have stepped ashore already knowing he was bound further west.

name: Gabriel Lambert, "Sieur de Sainte-Marie"
died: 1719, Lauzon, buried 25 Jul in St-Joseph church, aged 63 (Roy); tree: 24 Jul 1719
spouse: Françoise-Renée Roussel, daughter of the surgeon, m. 18 Jun 1683, contract 12 May 1683 before Rageot (Roy vol. 1 p. 258); tree: 18 Jun 1686
place: Habitation Sainte-Marie, Pointe-Lévy (between the Chaudière and the Etchemin, today Saint-Romuald)
life: He lived his whole life on the farm his father began clearing in 1652, "de mœurs douces et tranquilles"; when dragged into a family lawsuit he begged off, pleading his deafness, his little learning and the distance to town. The 1706-08 Catalogne map marks the place "M. Lambert ... la ferme Ste-Marie".
